note: Plain-language guides for different readers. Written from the FTC, FBI, ILO and UNODC guidance the checker uses; not yet reviewed by a practitioner.

audiences.title: For young people
audiences.who: Students, teenagers and anyone who meets people through games, apps and DMs.
signs: Someone you just met online asks for a photo, then threatens to send it to your friends or family unless you pay. That is sextortion. It is a crime against you, not something you did wrong.
A job that pays a lot for almost no work, especially if you must pay first or move to Telegram or WhatsApp to talk about it.
An older “friend” or partner who says your family won't understand, asks you to keep things secret, or wants to pick you up somewhere private.
A famous person in a video telling you to invest in crypto, or a giveaway where you only pay shipping. The video can be fake.
do: Don't pay, and don't send more pictures. Stop replying. Keep the messages.
Tell an adult you trust. You will not be in trouble. If images are already out, NCMEC's Take It Down can help remove them.
Check the offer here before you answer, or ask someone to check it with you.

audiences.title: For older adults
audiences.who: People over 60, who lose more money to scams than any other age group.
signs: A phone call in the voice of a grandchild or child saying they are in trouble and need money now, and asking you not to tell anyone. The voice can be copied by a computer.
Someone from “the bank”, “the government” or “tech support” asking you to move money to keep it safe, buy gift cards, or read out a code from your phone.
A new friend online who never meets in person, then needs money for a ticket, a hospital or an investment.
Any request that must happen today, in secret.
do: Hang up. Call the person or the bank back on a number you already have, not one they gave you.
Never pay with gift cards, crypto or a wire to someone you have not met. Banks and governments do not ask for those.
Agree a family code word for emergencies. Talk it over with someone before sending anything.

audiences.title: For families and carers
audiences.who: Parents, partners, friends and community workers worried about someone else.
signs: They have a new job, partner or “opportunity” they can't or won't describe, and they are suddenly secretive about their phone.
They are being asked to travel somewhere for work, with tickets and housing arranged by someone else, and no address they can share.
They have started sending money, buying gift cards or crypto, or asking to borrow money for fees.
They are pulling away from friends and family, or repeating lines like “you wouldn't understand”.
do: Stay in contact and stay calm. Shame keeps people quiet; blame makes it worse.
Run the check together on the message or offer, so the warning signs come from a neutral source, not from you.
Keep copies of names, numbers, addresses and travel details. If they go, that information is what helps find them.
If someone is being held or is in danger, call the hotline. You don't need proof.

audiences.title: For job seekers and migrant workers
audiences.who: Anyone offered work in another city or country, through an agent, an ad or a message.
signs: You are asked to pay recruitment fees, training fees or a deposit before you start. Real employers pay recruiters; workers should not.
The visa, the pay or the job described do not match what is on paper, or there is no contract at all.
Someone wants to hold your passport “for safekeeping”, or housing comes only with the job and its cost is taken from your wages.
The exact workplace address is only given on arrival, or the job is near known scam-compound areas.
do: Check the employer and the recruiter through official channels you find yourself: the company's own website, the labour ministry's licensed-agent list, the embassy.
Keep your passport. Keep copies of the contract, the ad and every message.
Tell someone at home the employer's name, the address, the flight and the agent's number before you travel.
If you are already there and cannot leave, contact your embassy or an IOM office. The hotline number works from abroad.
